questions.question_text: Which dilation takes the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the graph of $y=f(4x)$?

options.why: A factor $a$ inside $f$ gives factor $\tfrac1a$, so factor $\tfrac14$, not $4$.
A factor on the input $x$ is horizontal, not vertical.
A factor inside $f$ acts horizontally, not vertically.

questions.solution_text: $y=f(4x)$ has $a=4$, a horizontal dilation of factor $\dfrac14$.

questions.question_text: Which dilation takes the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the graph of $y=5f(x)$?

options.why: A factor outside $f$ acts on the outputs, so it is vertical.
The factor is outside $f$, so it is a vertical dilation, not horizontal.
Multiplying the output by $5$ gives factor $5$, not $\tfrac15$.

questions.solution_text: $y=5f(x)$ multiplies the output by $5$: a vertical dilation of factor $5$.

questions.question_text: Write the equation obtained when the graph of $y=x^{3}$ is dilated vertically by a factor of $2$.

options.why: Replacing $x$ with $2x$ gives $(2x)^{3}=8x^{3}$, a horizontal dilation rather than the requested vertical dilation.
This divides the output by $2$ instead of multiplying it by $2$.
This adds $2$ to the output instead of multiplying it by $2$.

questions.solution_text:
A vertical dilation of factor $2$ multiplies the output by $2$.
$y=2x^{3}$

options.why: The curve became steeper, so it stretched by factor $3$, not compressed.
That is $9x^{2}$; the marked point $(1,3)$ fits $3x^{2}$, not $9x^{2}$.
The point $(0,0)$ stayed on the curve, so it was stretched, not slid up.

questions.solution_text:
The $x$-coordinate stayed and the $y$-coordinate tripled: $(x,y)\to(x,3y)$.
Vertical dilation of factor $3$, $y=3x^{2}$.

questions.question_text: For $f(x)=x^{2}$ and $g(x)=16x^{2}$, which pair of dilations both take the graph of $f$ to the graph of $g$?

options.why: Horizontal factor $4$ gives $f(x/4)=x^{2}/16$, reversing the required horizontal compression.
Vertical factor $4$ gives $4x^{2}$; it confuses the input multiplier $4$ with the output multiplier $16$.
Horizontal factor $\dfrac1{16}$ gives $f(16x)=256x^{2}$; it uses the output multiplier as the input multiplier without taking its square root.

questions.solution_text:
$g(x)=16f(x)$, so the vertical dilation has factor $16$.
Also, $g(x)=(4x)^{2}=f(4x)$, so the horizontal dilation has factor $\dfrac14$.
Both descriptions give $y=16x^{2}$.

questions.question_text: State the direction and factor of the dilation that gives $y=f\!\left(\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)$ from $y=f(x)$.

options.why: This uses the inside multiplier $\dfrac23$ instead of its reciprocal $\dfrac32$.
This treats the inside multiplier as a multiplier of the output.
This takes the reciprocal correctly but gives the wrong direction: the multiplier is on the input inside $f$.

questions.solution_text:
The inside factor is $a=\dfrac23$, so the dilation factor is $\dfrac1a=\dfrac32$.
Horizontal dilation of factor $\dfrac32$.

options.why: The factor is $6\div2=3$, found by dividing, not subtracting.
Horizontal factor $3$ gives $2(x/3)^{2}=2x^{2}/9$, not $6x^{2}$. A horizontal factor $1/\sqrt3$ would give $2(\sqrt3 x)^{2}=6x^{2}$.
The curve became steeper, a stretch by $3$, not a compression.

questions.solution_text:
$6x^{2}=3\,(2x^{2})$
The output is multiplied by $3$: a vertical dilation of factor $3$.

questions.question_text: Identify a suitable dilation that takes $y=\dfrac{1}{x-3}$ to $y=\dfrac{1}{3x-3}$.

options.why: This uses the input multiplier $3$ as the dilation factor instead of taking its reciprocal.
This divides the entire output by $3$, giving $1/(3x-9)$ rather than $1/(3x-3)$.
This multiplies the output by $3$, giving $3/(x-3)$ rather than replacing the input $x$ with $3x$.

questions.solution_text:
For $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-3}$, $f(3x)=\dfrac{1}{3x-3}$.
The input multiplier is $3$: horizontal dilation of factor $\dfrac13$.
